clue.text: Ace meals on a ship

blocks.note: the card's own letter, the one printed in its corner
board is the food half of room and board — what a landlady provides at table

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the surface points to the sea: 'Ace meals' reads as a compliment about the catering, which is exactly where the two pieces are standing.
explanation.definitionFit: on a ship → ABOARD: the everyday word for being carried by a vessel once you have stepped off the quay.

clue.text: Stand back! Mirror, perversely, is not online

indicators.note: To do a thing perversely is to do it contrarily, against the way it was meant to go, so the letters refuse the order they were handed in.

blocks.note: an exclamation and a newspaper title, fifteen letters between them — exactly the fifteen the entry needs

explanation.walkthrough: The italics make Mirror a newspaper, and both it and 'Stand back!' promise a reversal. Neither delivers: they are fodder, and 'perversely' is the clue's only instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: not online → BRICKS-AND-MORTAR: the trade's adjective for a shop or bank with a physical building, as against one that exists only on the web.

clue.text: Graceless sabre-rattler not starting to usher in war dead

indicators.note: A word that does not start has lost the letter it begins with, so the bird named beside this arrives without its H.
An usher walks ahead of the people he brings through the door, so the trimmed piece leads and everything else is written behind it.

blocks.note: a hawk is the warmonger of the political aviary, and the bird is taken minus the letter it opens with
the clue's own word, lifted whole and unaltered
d is the standard short form of dead, as printed on a family tree

explanation.walkthrough: Sabre-rattling is threatening war rather than making it, and the hawk is the bird that kind of talk belongs to. The definition hides at the front, looking like scene-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Graceless → AWKWARD: clumsy in movement or manner, the sense of someone who cannot cross a room without knocking something over.

clue.text: Spiritual leader in a state, a chap's written up

indicators.note: In a down entry, writing something up means setting it down from the bottom square, so the assembled letters are read back towards the first.

blocks.note: the article, then Mali, the landlocked West African republic
the article again, then the informal word for a young man

explanation.walkthrough: Read from the bottom, the four small pieces regroup entirely: the joins in the wordplay fall nowhere near the join between the answer's two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Spiritual leader → DALAI LAMA: the title of Tibetan Buddhism's foremost teacher, an office rather than a name, so it defines a leader by religious rank.

clue.text: You shouldn't have got into setter, perhaps Everyman's beginning to show feebleness

indicators.note: Something that gets into a thing ends up within it rather than beside it, so the polite two letters are planted inside the piece already assembled.
The beginning of a word is the letter it opens with, and only that one letter is taken from the byline this puzzle carries.

blocks.note: a setter is one breed among many, so the general animal is wanted — 'perhaps' marks the example
the opening letter of the name this puzzle is signed with
what you say on being handed an unexpected present is thanks, and this is the two-letter British version of it

explanation.walkthrough: Everyman signs his own puzzles, so his name in a clue usually means him; here it is only its first letter, and the setter that matters is the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: feebleness → DOTAGE: the doddering weakness of extreme old age, a noun for the state itself rather than for the years that brought it on.

clue.text: Drop in moat?

blocks.note: the verb: to drop a plan, a habit or a passenger is to abandon it and move on
the noun: the trench dug round a castle wall, water in it or not, is one sort of this

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, and the surface is one continuous picture — a drop of water in a moat — so nothing at all marks the place where the first meaning stops.
explanation.definitionFit: Drop → DITCH as a verb, to abandon something; moat → DITCH by example, a moat being one kind of trench dug for defence.

clue.text: Those people: one soldier; three kings

blocks.note: the pronoun you would use for those people if you were pointing at them
one soldier is a soldier — the article does the counting
GI is the American enlisted man of every war film

explanation.walkthrough: 'Those people' and 'one soldier' read as a sentence about troops, and the semicolon does a comma's work: three separate pieces, laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: three kings → THE MAGI: the visitors who brought gifts at the nativity, called kings by carol and tradition though scripture gives them neither rank nor number.

clue.text: Experience mishap when visiting geyser?

blocks.note: to visit a place is to enter it, the phrase you would use of a house you finally managed to reach
an Icelandic geyser is a jet of exactly that, thrown boiling out of the ground — one example standing for the general thing

explanation.walkthrough: The trouble idiom and the tourist attraction are the same four words, which is the whole joke: a literal visit to one would land you in the figurative other.
explanation.definitionFit: Experience mishap → GET INTO HOT WATER: the idiom for landing yourself in trouble, where the trouble is usually somebody else's anger.

clue.text: Startled kittens bolt in psych procedure

indicators.note: A startled animal runs in whatever direction it happens to be facing, and letters given that fright land in an order nobody chose.

blocks.note: eleven letters of frightened cat, which is exactly the eleven the entry needs

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a vet's waiting room and the answer is a psychologist's couch. Note where the anagram indicator sits: first word, passing for scene-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: psych procedure → INK-BLOT TEST: the Rorschach method, where what a patient sees in a symmetrical smudge is read back as personality.

clue.text: Foul air from small cat

blocks.note: S is the size on a clothing label
a mog, or moggy, is British household slang for a cat of no particular breed

explanation.walkthrough: Two ordinary words with nothing odd about either, which is the difficulty: nothing in 'small cat' announces that it is spelling rather than describing.
explanation.definitionFit: Foul air → SMOG: the choking blend of smoke and fog that settles over a city, so the definition names it by what it does to the lungs.

clue.text: Major port in Pasadena

indicators.note: The small word is doing real work rather than joining: what the definition wants is sitting inside the word that follows, not near it.

blocks.note: four consecutive letters inside the Californian city's name, beginning at its third

explanation.walkthrough: A Californian suburb with a Yemeni harbour buried in it, and no comma or hyphen to mark the seam — long place names are a hidden word's favourite cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Major port → ADEN: the great harbour at the mouth of the Red Sea, for centuries the coaling stop on the route between Europe and India.

clue.text: Birthday announcement pathetic, a mawkish constant

definitions.note: The answer is an instruction called out at the party rather than a noun; the setter defines it by naming the moment at which those words get announced.

indicators.note: Something pathetic is in a sorry, fallen-apart state, and letters in that condition cannot be relied on to stay where they were put.

blocks.note: eight of the nine letters, taken from the article and the adjective as they stand
e is the mathematician's constant, 2.718..., joining the shuffle as a single letter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Pathetic' looks like a verdict on the birthday card and is the instruction instead. Everyman enjoys an anagram whose fodder reads as an insult.
explanation.definitionFit: Birthday announcement → MAKE A WISH: the words called out over the candles, the standard invitation at the moment the cake is carried in.

clue.text: Spotty old hat for a Cockney

indicators.note: London's East End accent drops the aitch from the front of a word, and what is left has to be judged by ear rather than by spelling.

blocks.note: anything old hat has been worn out by overuse, which is what this longer word means
with the aitch gone, what is left is said exactly as the much shorter spelling is, though the two share barely half their letters

explanation.walkthrough: Say 'hackneyed' without its aitch and you have said the answer. The joke is that a Cockney's 'old hat' turns out to describe a teenager's complexion.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotty → ACNED: covered in the pimples of acne, the doctor's adjective for the skin the playground calls spotty.

clue.text: He's related Greek saga's finale including, additionally, prince

indicators.note: A finale is the last thing to happen, so only the letter the word ends on is taken from it.
To include a thing is to hold it within, so the two pieces named afterwards drop into the middle of what came before.

blocks.note: Gr is the standard short form for Greek, and Greece's international car plate
one thing additionally to another is one and another
P is the abbreviation for prince, as on a royal monogram
the last letter of sagA

explanation.walkthrough: Everything after the definition reads like literary criticism — a Greek epic, its ending, a prince — and every word of it is an abbreviation or a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: He's related → GRANDPA: the familiar name for a parent's father, so the definition points at a particular male relative rather than at kinship in general.

clue.text: Unlisted (not indexed) company offering riches nowadays, primarily?

definitions.text: Unlisted (not indexed) company offering riches nowadays, primarily?

indicators.note: Primarily means before anything else, so each word in front of it gives up the letter it opens with and nothing more.

blocks.clueFragment: Unlisted (not indexed) company offering riches nowadays
blocks.note: the opening letter of each of these seven words in turn, the bracketed pair counting exactly like the rest

explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: the sentence describes a private company worth a fortune and spells it at the same time. The brackets are the only thing making the count awkward.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue reads straight: a start-up valued past a billion but never floated on any exchange is precisely an unlisted, unindexed firm promising sudden riches.

clue.text: Turned out, sadly, to be ignorant

indicators.note: To say a thing happened sadly is to say it went wrong, and letters that have gone wrong end up somewhere other than their proper places.

blocks.note: the nine letters of the opening phrase, re-sorted

explanation.walkthrough: 'Turned out' wants to be the instruction — turning is exactly what setters ask for — but here it is the material, and the meek adverb beside it does the ordering.
explanation.definitionFit: ignorant → UNTUTORED: never taught, and so lacking what schooling would have supplied — ignorance by absence of instruction rather than by stupidity.

clue.text: Part of Finland - or, rather, another country

indicators.note: Only a piece of what follows is wanted, so a run of letters inside those words is being pointed at, not their meaning.

blocks.note: seven consecutive letters running from inside the first country's name through the aside that follows it

explanation.walkthrough: A dash and two commas fall inside the run and not one of them interrupts it: punctuation is invisible to a hidden word, which is what makes this one hard to see.
explanation.definitionFit: another country → ANDORRA: the tiny Pyrenean principality between France and Spain, 'another' because the clue's own letters have already named one.

clue.text: Help with a passport, perhaps as embassy opens

indicators.note: What opens a word is the letter it starts with, so the building named beside this hands over one letter and keeps the rest.

blocks.note: the article, then the two letters any document proving who you are is called — a passport being one example
the first letter of the building named here

explanation.walkthrough: Passport and embassy are both there for the travel picture, and only one of them survives as a whole piece of wordplay; the other is cut to a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Help → AIDE: a person employed to assist somebody important, and 'help' names a person too when it means the staff rather than the act.

clue.text: Rush around California airport that's restful

indicators.note: To go around a thing is to enclose it, so the piece named first opens up and the letters that follow are set inside it.

blocks.note: a rush is a marsh plant, and the setter wants the other tall stem that grows in the same wet ground
LAX is the three-letter code for Los Angeles International, printed on every bag tag

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rush' is the trap: it reads as speed and it is a plant. Airport codes are worth collecting — three letters, used the way setters use chemical symbols.
explanation.definitionFit: restful → RELAXED: at ease, with nothing tensed; both words describe an absence of strain rather than any actual sleep.

clue.text: Wearisome after time, editor with promises of payment

blocks.note: T is the standard short form of time, as on a stopwatch
Ed is the newspaper's editor, the form used on a masthead
an IOU is a scribbled promise to pay, and more than one of them takes the plural

explanation.walkthrough: Three abbreviations in a row, dressed as a complaint about the office. IOU is worth knowing — 'I owe you' spelled by its sound — because setters use it constantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Wearisome → TEDIOUS: long, dull and repetitive, so wearying by sheer monotony rather than by effort — the meeting that will not end.

clue.text: Rodents cut up - headless worm inside

indicators.note: A headless word has lost the letter at its front, so the crawler named beside this arrives without its W.
What is inside sits within rather than alongside, so the trimmed piece is planted in the middle of the other.

blocks.note: to cut something up into small cubes is to dice it
the wriggler minus the letter it starts with

explanation.walkthrough: In a down entry 'cut up' promises a reversal and delivers a kitchen verb instead. The dash is Everyman separating the halves without saying anything.
explanation.definitionFit: Rodents → DORMICE: the plural of the small hibernating mouse with the furry tail, rodents by family and famously asleep at Alice's tea party.

clue.text: I'm surprised map-maker's upset part of London

indicators.note: To upset a thing is to turn it over, and in a down entry the letters turned over are read from the bottom square upwards.

blocks.note: the noise you make when something takes you unawares
the Ordnance Survey is Britain's national mapping agency, known everywhere by its two initials

explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reads as annoyed, describing the poor cartographer, and is really the instruction: read the two pieces from the bottom of the entry upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: part of London → SOHO: the square of streets north of Shaftesbury Avenue, long the capital's district for clubs, restaurants and the film trade.

clue.text: On reflection, Liberal parliamentarian is amusing

indicators.note: A reflection shows a thing the other way round, so what follows is taken from its far end back to its start.

blocks.note: L is the ballot paper's abbreviation for Liberal
a member of Britain's upper house sits in Parliament without ever having been elected to it

explanation.walkthrough: 'On reflection' opens the clue as a phrase about second thoughts, which is how a reversal indicator likes to arrive: sounding like a comment on the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: amusing → DROLL: funny in a dry, understated way, the adjective for wit that raises an eyebrow rather than a laugh.

clue.text: How gut-rot's provoked?

indicators.note: To provoke is to stir something up, and letters stirred up settle in an arrangement nobody planned.

blocks.note: the nine letters of the question's opening, re-sorted

explanation.walkthrough: An all-in-one: the same words ask the question and spell the answer. Gut-rot is British slang for cheap spirits, the sort that burn on the way down.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: what grows out of something else as its consequence is what a rough drink's after-effects amount to.

clue.text: In a weird way, how number's found in the end?

definitions.text: how number's found in the end

blocks.note: the plain adverb: strangely, in a manner that does not fit what was expected

blocks.clueFragment: how number's found in the end
blocks.note: count through the letters of 'the end' and take the first, third and fifth: T, E, N, a number sitting at the positions the answer is named for

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a puzzle in miniature: 'the end' holds TEN if you take alternate letters from the start, and the answer names the way you had to read.
explanation.definitionFit: In a weird way → ODDLY, the plain adverb for strangely; and a number picked out of 'the end' at alternate letters is found in exactly that manner.

clue.text: Stuffy type occupied with relics of the past?

definitions.text: Stuffy type occupied with relics of the past?

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: a pompous bore in an airless room, the sort who lectures you about antiques

blocks.clueFragment: occupied with relics of the past
blocks.note: the setter means it literally — the work is done on creatures that stopped being alive some time ago

explanation.walkthrough: 'Stuffy' does two jobs at once: the adjective for a boring man, and the verb for what this trade actually does to a dead fox before it goes on the wall.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue describes the answer the long way round: this is the one profession where being called a stuffy sort surrounded by dead animals is simply accurate.

clue.text: Good is the one that comes yearly

definitions.text: Good is the one that comes yearly

blocks.note: the reading the surface pushes: an adjective praising whichever one is meant, as though several were being compared
a weekday comes round every seven days; fix the right word in front of it and the name belongs to a single date in the church calendar

explanation.walkthrough: The joke is the capital G: as a label rather than praise, it turns an ordinary weekday into the solemn day before Easter, which comes once a year.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue defines the answer sideways: only with 'Good' fixed in front of it does this day name an annual observance instead of a weekly one.

clue.text: Gloomy and arid, capturing attention

indicators.note: To capture a thing is to take it prisoner and hold on to it, so the shorter piece ends up trapped inside the longer one.

blocks.note: arid ground has no moisture left in it at all
to lend an ear, or to have someone's ear, is to give or be given attention

explanation.walkthrough: 'Capturing' is the only instruction and it arrives late: the first three words read as two adjectives sharing a comma, which is how the container stays hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloomy → DREARY: dull, grey and spirit-lowering, the word for a wet November afternoon rather than for anything actively sad.
